title: How to Organize Reference Images for Design Work
description: Organize reference images for your next design: a practical workflow, a PureRef, Eagle, Milanote and FloatBoard comparison, and tips for keeping notes beside images.
alt: FloatBoard in dark mode displaying four landscape image references in a two-column grid
caption: A four-image board keeps a small set of references visible together. This screenshot shows the FloatBoard image layout; the workflow below is an illustrative example.
intro: To organize reference images for design work, keep your original files in a searchable project folder, then choose a small working set for the decision in front of you. This guide is for designers and illustrators who need to compare composition, light or visual direction while drawing. It walks through a four-image example in FloatBoard and explains when PureRef, Eagle or Milanote may fit better.

sections.title: Start with a design question, not a pile of pictures
sections.html:
Before adding images, write one sentence describing the decision you need to make. For example: ‘Choose a warm evening palette with a quiet, open composition.’ This gives every image a job. One might show the light, another the amount of empty space, and another the contrast between foreground and background.

The screenshot above contains four different landscapes. For this example, the coastal sunset can be a reference for warm light, the palm scene for reflections, the mountain scene for silhouette, and the darker landscape for contrast. Those are observations to compare, not four instructions to reproduce in one design.

If you cannot explain why an image is on your board, leave it in your source folder for now. A small board that answers one question is easier to use than a larger board whose images compete for attention.

sections.title: Keep reference images and notes visible in FloatBoard
sections.html:
1. Keep the originals. Save your source files in a project folder. Treat the board as a working reference, not your only archive.
  2. Choose a few distinct references. Avoid filling the board with almost identical images. Pick the examples that reveal different aspects of your question.
  3. Add the images to FloatBoard. Use the image workflow available in your installed version. The image panel keeps the references together, as shown in the screenshot.
  4. Place the window beside your canvas. Use the pin / always-on-top control so the board remains visible when you return to the design app. Leave enough space for the actual work.
  5. Add a short reference note. In the text panel, write the design question and one observation per image. Keep copied client wording labelled separately from your own ideas; a clipboard fragment needs its source and context.
  6. Check readability. If important details are too small, work with fewer references or use a larger view. A tiny thumbnail is suitable for overall composition, but not fine typography or texture.

FloatBoard’s free plan has image limits. Check the current plan details before planning a larger collection; this workflow does not require filling every available slot.

sections.title: Record what each reference teaches you
sections.html:
Images alone do not preserve the reasoning behind a design. Keep a short note in your project document with three fields: source, detail to study, and decision. For example: ‘Coastal sunset — warm highlights against a darker foreground — try a warm accent on a neutral background.’

Save the source URL and any usage or licensing information with the original. Collecting an image for reference does not give you permission to publish it. When it is time to deliver the project, choose assets you own or have permission to use.

After each design pass, write down which reference helped. If two images now serve the same purpose, keep the clearer one on the working board. This makes the next pass a focused comparison instead of another round of browsing.

sections.title: Fix the common problems before adding more images
sections.html:
The board covers your work: move or resize it rather than squeezing your canvas into the remaining space. On a small screen, it can be more useful to compare two images at a time.

You keep collecting but do not decide: return to the opening question. Choose one visual direction, make a small draft, and compare that draft against your references. The board supports a decision; it does not make one.

You need precise color values: return to the original asset and your design app’s color tools. A scaled screenshot or thumbnail should not be treated as an authoritative color measurement.

sections.title: Tools for this workflow: PureRef, Eagle, Milanote or FloatBoard?
sections.html:
Choose a reference image organizer by the job you need it to do. Keeping pictures above your canvas, finding an old asset and presenting a mood board are different needs. The suggestions below are based on the linked product documentation, checked on 24 September 2026; they are not a hands-on comparison or a speed benchmark. This guide is published by FloatBoard.

For asset retrieval, investigate Eagle; for shared feedback, investigate Milanote. These tools are not interchangeable replacements for every PureRef feature.

sections.title: Is PureRef free? Check the license before choosing an alternative
sections.html:
PureRef’s download page currently offers a custom contribution amount for its personal, hobbyist and educational license, and separate paid commercial options. Do not assume that personal-use terms cover paid client work; check the current download options and license agreement for your situation.

If you want to try a different workflow without paying first, FloatBoard has the limited free plan described above. Milanote’s free plan includes 100 notes, images or links and 10 file uploads. Those limits measure different things, so compare them against your actual project rather than treating either as an unlimited reference library.

sections.title: Frequently asked questions about organizing reference images
sections.html:
What is the best way to organize reference images?

Separate storage from active reference. Keep original files and source links in project folders, use descriptive names or tags for retrieval, and bring only the images needed for the current decision onto your working board. For example, tag an image by what you need to find later—lighting, composition or material—not just “inspiration.”

Is there a free alternative to PureRef?

For a small mixed board of notes and images, you can try FloatBoard’s free plan. For a shareable mood board, Milanote has a free tier. Neither choice reproduces every PureRef feature; choose based on whether you need a visible reference, an asset library or collaboration, and check the limits above.

How do I keep reference images visible while drawing?

Use an always-on-top reference window, position it beside your canvas and switch back to the drawing app to check the layout. FloatBoard and PureRef support this approach. If the board hides your tools, reduce the working set or move it to another display.

Can I keep design notes beside my reference images?

Yes. FloatBoard’s text and image panels can share a window. Try one note containing your brief, source links and the next decision beside a few selected images. For longer written work, follow the guide to keeping reference notes visible; for interface work, see code snippets and screenshots while debugging.

sections.title: Try the workflow with your next design task
sections.html:
Download FloatBoard, choose up to four reference images and add one note describing the decision you are making. Pin the board beside your design app, make a draft, then remove any reference that no longer helps. Keep final decisions in your project document so they survive beyond this working set.

If copied instructions are what you lose most often, explore the clipboard manager workflow. If your priority is written reminders above other windows, start with floating desktop notes. Use the board for the material you need in sight now.

title: How to Debug UI Bugs with Code Snippets and Screenshots
description: Keep a screenshot, code snippet and expected result together while debugging UI bugs. Compare FloatBoard with snippet managers for this specific workflow.
alt: FloatBoard with four image thumbnails on the left and a text card containing HTML markup on the right
caption: FloatBoard can show image references and text side by side. The HTML in this screenshot is a reference snippet, not an executable code editor.
intro: If you are debugging a visual bug, a searchable code snippet manager and a visible reference board solve different problems. Keep reusable code in your repository or snippet library; put the screenshot, the few relevant lines and the expected result in view for the bug you are fixing now. Here is a repeatable UI-debugging workflow, followed by an honest comparison with massCode, Pieces and Cacher.

sections.title: Start with one reproducible UI bug
sections.html:
First write down the action that triggers the bug, the viewport or window size and what actually happens. Then record the expected behavior. A screenshot without these details can look convincing but leave a teammate unable to reproduce anything.

Keep the screenshot in your issue or project folder, where it will still be available after this working session. Copy only the smallest relevant markup or CSS fragment onto your temporary board. Label it with the file path and component name so you can return to the authoritative source.

Do not paste access tokens, customer data or private URLs into a board that may appear in a screen share. Redact the screenshot before sharing it.

sections.title: Put a screenshot and code snippet side by side
sections.html:
1. Capture the visual symptom. Make one screenshot at the size where the problem appears. Keep the original in the bug report.
  2. Copy the relevant snippet. Add its file path and a brief note about why you suspect it. A text card is a reference, not a synchronized copy of the source file.
  3. Add both to FloatBoard. Put the screenshot in the image panel and the snippet plus expected result in the text panel. The image above shows this mixed layout.
  4. Pin the board beside the editor. Keep it in view while the editor and browser remain the tools you use to change and test the code.
  5. Change one likely cause and reproduce again. Replace the working note with the new observation; do not stack unexplained copies of the same snippet.

This is useful when you need a snippet manager with images for the immediate task. FloatBoard is not a searchable code library or an IDE: it does not run code, highlight syntax or keep pasted text in sync with Git.

sections.title: Example: debug an overflowing image grid at 390px
sections.html:
Suppose a gallery extends past its container on a narrow screen. The note below keeps the question, evidence and next check together. It is an illustrative checklist, not a diagnosis of FloatBoard or a universal CSS fix.

Bug: image cards overflow the gallery panel
Reproduce: open the gallery at a 390px viewport
Actual: horizontal scrolling appears
Expected: cards stay inside the panel
Source: styles/gallery.css, .gallery-grid
Evidence: screenshot saved in issue #123
Next check: grid columns, item min-width, image sizing

In DevTools, inspect the actual grid and its children. If a child cannot shrink, test whether its minimum size causes the overflow; if the column definition is fixed, test a responsive layout. Keep the before and after screenshots at the same viewport. The fix belongs in the source and its test, not in the reference note.

sections.title: Snippet manager or floating board? Choose by the job
sections.html:
A code snippet manager is a better place for examples you want to search and reuse next month. A floating board is for the few references you must compare while fixing one bug today. This is a feature-and-use-case comparison based on the linked product documentation, checked on 28 September 2026; we did not benchmark the competing apps. FloatBoard publishes this guide.

Where to keep snippets and screenshots

PiecesYou need capture and retrieval features beyond a small working board.Pieces documents image pasting and code extraction from screenshots. Check its current product and plan before choosing it.
CacherYou want a searchable code library, editor integrations or team snippets. Its documentation describes search and insertion.Its attachments support pasted images. Do not assume a snippet manager cannot store screenshots.

Looking for a massCode alternative or a Pieces alternative? If the missing feature is search, tagging or long-term snippet reuse, FloatBoard is not a direct replacement. If your problem is losing the screenshot while changing CSS, try a mixed reference board alongside your existing snippet library. Dash is another documentation and snippet tool, primarily for macOS, when API reference lookup is the main job.

sections.title: Use clipboard history for retrieval, the board for comparison
sections.html:
A clipboard manager can preserve recently copied material, including images in some products. A saved snippet adds information such as title, language and source. A floating board keeps selected material visible. These are different roles, and one app can support more than one role.

FloatBoard combines recent text clipboard history with a visible text-and-image board. The board lets you compare a screenshot with a pasted code fragment, but its clipboard history is not a versioned snippet library. Always compare an older clip with the current source before reusing it. See the clipboard workflow for the product details.

sections.title: Questions developers ask about snippets and screenshots
sections.html:
What is the best way to organize code snippets?

Keep production code in the repository. Save genuinely reusable fragments in a searchable snippet manager with a descriptive title, language, source link and date or version. Keep temporary debugging fragments in a small task board, then remove them when the issue is resolved.

Can a clipboard manager store images?

Some can; capabilities differ by product. FloatBoard lets you add images to its visible board and has recent text clipboard history. Do not assume its history stores every image you have copied. For a screenshot you must preserve, save the original in your project or issue tracker.

Is there a free alternative to Pieces for snippets?

massCode is a free, open-source snippet library, according to its official site. FloatBoard has a limited free plan for visible text-and-image references, but is not a Pieces replacement for searchable snippets or image-to-code extraction. Compare current plans and features on each official site.

What is the best code snippet manager for Windows?

There is no single best choice for every workflow. For a searchable local library, compare massCode with Cacher; for screenshot-to-code features, examine Pieces. For keeping a screenshot and the few relevant lines visible while you edit, FloatBoard can complement those tools. Try the task you actually repeat before committing your whole library.

sections.title: Keep the fix, clear the temporary board
sections.html:
When the issue is fixed, record the reproduction steps, changed file and before-and-after evidence in the issue or pull request. Store reusable snippets in the repository or a searchable library. Remove temporary references that no longer explain the task.

Try FloatBoard for a small UI debugging task with one screenshot, one snippet and one expected result. If the real pain is research notes rather than code, see the writing reference workflow.

title: How to Keep Research Notes Visible While Writing
description: Keep research notes beside Word or Google Docs without losing sources. Compare split screen, PowerToys and FloatBoard, then use a source-card template.
alt: FloatBoard showing text reference cards on the left and six image thumbnails on the right
caption: Text and image references can share a FloatBoard window. The screenshot shows the layout; the writing example below uses its own illustrative notes.
intro: To keep research notes visible while writing, separate the source from your own wording, then place only the two or three notes needed for the next paragraph beside your draft. On Windows you can use split screen, pin a notes window with PowerToys or use a purpose-built floating board. This guide shows when each works and how to avoid losing attribution while you write.

sections.title: Choose the notes needed for the next paragraph
sections.html:
Start with the claim you are about to write. Choose the source detail you must verify, a short quotation if exact wording matters and the question that paragraph should answer. Leave the rest of your research in its original library or project folder.

A useful working note answers four questions: where did this come from, when was it published or checked, what does it actually say, and how will I use it? A floating note is a prompt to check the original source, not a citation by itself.

For an image you plan to describe, record its source and what detail matters. The screenshot above shows FloatBoard text cards beside image thumbnails, but a text-only writing task does not need images.

sections.title: Three ways to keep notes beside Word or Google Docs
sections.html:
Use the least complicated setup that leaves your draft readable. These options solve the same visibility problem at different levels; the feature descriptions come from the linked product documentation, checked on 28 September 2026. This article is published by FloatBoard.

Choose a note setup for a writing session
SetupBest fitTrade-off
Split screenTwo windows are enough and you have room for both. Put the original source or notes beside your draft.On a narrow display, each window may become too small to read comfortably.
PowerToys Always On TopOn Windows, pin a notes window above the draft with the default Win+Ctrl+T shortcut.It pins an existing window; you still need to choose a notes app and keep source details organized yourself.
FloatBoardKeep short text notes and optional image reminders in one small window, then use its pin control while writing.It is a working board, not a citation manager or searchable research archive. The free plan includes 5 texts and 5 images per day.

Open the draft first. Place the reference so it does not cover the sentence you are editing. Switch back to the writing app and confirm the note stays visible. If it blocks the document, reduce the working set or use split screen instead.

sections.title: Copy this source-card structure before drafting
sections.html:
Imagine drafting a short product comparison. The following is a template, not a claim about any specific product:

Claim to check: [one factual statement]
Source: [author or organization + page title + URL]
Published/checked: [date shown by source / date you checked]
Exact wording: "[brief quotation, if needed]"
My paraphrase: [your own wording, clearly labelled]
Where it goes: [draft section or paragraph]
Before publishing: reopen source and verify context

Put the source and exact wording in one labelled note; keep your interpretation separately. If the page has changed, update the note from the original rather than trusting an old clipboard fragment. For product details about FloatBoard itself, verify against the feature overview, current plan and download page.

sections.title: Do not let a floating note become a lost citation
sections.html:
Use quotation marks for words copied exactly. Keep the original URL, author or organization and relevant publication date with the quote. When you paraphrase, compare your sentence with the full source passage; a short clipped phrase can reverse the meaning of a qualification.

For academic or citation-heavy writing, use a dedicated reference manager. Zotero integrates with word processors and can insert citations and bibliographies. FloatBoard does not replace that source library; it can hold a small visible working set while you consult Zotero or your documents.

If you are working with private correspondence or sensitive research, keep it out of screenshots that you share publicly. Only place material on the working board that is appropriate for that workspace.

sections.title: Frequently asked questions about visible writing notes
sections.html:
How can I keep notes always on top while writing in Windows?

Open your notes app and use Microsoft PowerToys Always On Top to pin its active window, or use FloatBoard’s own pin control. Resize the note window so Word or your browser stays readable.

Can I keep reference notes beside Google Docs?

Yes. Google Docs runs in a browser window, so you can place a separate notes window beside it or keep a small FloatBoard window pinned above it. If your screen is narrow, a side-by-side layout may work better than an overlapping note.

Should I use a floating note or Zotero for research?

Use Zotero or another reference manager for the source collection and final citations. Use a floating note for the few facts or questions you need in view during the current paragraph. A source card on the board should always point back to the original.

How do I avoid accidentally copying source text into my draft?

Label exact quotations and your own paraphrases differently. Draft from the source idea with the original closed or beside you, then reopen it to verify accuracy and attribution before publishing.

sections.title: Review the draft, then refresh the working set
sections.html:
At the end of the section, reopen each source and verify names, dates, numbers, qualifications and quotations. Move any lasting note into your source library or project document. Replace the temporary references with those needed for the next section.

Try FloatBoard with two source cards beside a draft, then decide whether a visible board improves your writing setup. If you mainly need to recover copied text, see the clipboard history guide; if you are comparing visual ideas, see the image reference workflow.

title: Windows Clipboard History: Copy Multiple Items and Keep Notes Visible
description: Learn how to use Win + V for copied text and images, troubleshoot missing clipboard items, and choose when floating notes help with an active task.
alt: FloatBoard window showing separate text cards beside a grid of image thumbnails
caption: FloatBoard displays text and image references together. This product screenshot illustrates the layout; it is not the Windows clipboard history panel.
intro: Press Windows + V to open clipboard history on Windows and reuse something you copied earlier. If you need instructions to stay in sight while completing a task, keep a short note in a separate visible window. This guide shows how to use both approaches, how to investigate missing clipboard entries, and how to avoid turning a temporary clipboard into your only record.

sections.title: How to copy and paste multiple items with Windows + V
sections.html:
1. Press Windows + V and turn on clipboard history if prompted.
  2. Copy a short piece of text, then copy a different one.
  3. Click where you want to insert the first item, reopen Windows + V, and select it.
  4. Repeat for another item. Check what was inserted before moving to the next field.

Microsoft documents a 25-entry history and a 4 MB limit per item, supporting text, HTML and bitmap formats. You can pin entries you want to retain. See Microsoft’s clipboard instructions, checked on 29 September 2026. These limits describe Windows clipboard history, not FloatBoard.

sections.title: Clipboard history or floating notes: which fits your task?
sections.html:
Choose by what you need to do next. Pasting a previously copied address is different from reading a checklist while you fill in a form. This comparison is published by FloatBoard and describes documented roles, not a performance benchmark.

Three ways to work with copied information
NeedUseful starting pointKeep in mind
Paste an earlier copyWindows clipboard historySelect an entry when you need to paste; check history limits.
Read a few notes while workingFloatBoard’s floating text and image windowKeep only the references for the current task; check plan limits.
Keep a lasting project recordYour project document or notes librarySave sources, final wording and decisions where you can find them later.

You can use clipboard history and a visible note together. There is no need to move your entire history into a board.

sections.title: Example: prepare a product listing without mixing up fields
sections.html:
Imagine updating a listing with an approved name, a short description and an image. The goal is to check each field against its source while editing. The following is an illustrative workflow, not a report of a measured time saving.

  1. Open the approved source document and the listing editor.
  2. Create a small FloatBoard text note with labels for the title, description and items to verify.
  3. Add the relevant image reference if you need to check the selected picture. Keep the original file for the actual upload.
  4. Use the board’s pin control and position the window beside the editor. Switch back to the editor to confirm the note stays visible.
  5. Paste each field, using Windows clipboard history when helpful, then compare the result against the labelled note.
  6. Read the final preview and save the approved version in the project document.
LISTING CHECK
Title: [approved wording]
Description source: [document / section]
Image: [original filename]
Before saving: spelling, selected image, required fields

Labels matter: two similar copied sentences can belong to different products. Keep one listing’s working set on screen at a time.

sections.title: Why is an item missing from Windows clipboard history?
sections.html:
First check whether history was enabled when you copied it. Then check the item’s format and size. An older entry may have been displaced by the history limit. Microsoft also notes that restarting clears unpinned history. Its clipboard support page explains pinning and clearing entries.

If a particular image does not appear, keep its original file and insert it through the destination app’s image command. Do not keep recopying a large file and assume the history panel will store it. If the entry appears but the pasted result looks wrong, inspect the destination’s paste options and compare against the source.

A visible reference is useful for checking the result, but it cannot repair an unsupported clipboard format or reconstruct information that was never saved.

sections.title: Keep the working set small and labelled
sections.html:
Before a new task, remove references that belong to the previous one. Preserve anything important in your project files first. Avoid copying passwords or other secrets into a board that might appear in a screen share.

FloatBoard’s free plan currently allows five texts and five images per day and one window. A note containing a few labelled fields is enough to try this workflow. This article does not claim that FloatBoard provides Windows clipboard synchronization or an unlimited free history.

sections.title: Questions about clipboard history and floating notes
sections.html:
Does Windows + V show everything I have ever copied?

No. It is a limited history, not a permanent archive. Keep important material in a saved document and use the history for recent copied items.

Can clipboard history contain images?

Windows clipboard history supports bitmap content within its size limit. That does not mean every copied image or file format will be stored. Keep the original image when you need dependable access.

Can I keep copied text visible without repeatedly opening the history?

Put the relevant text in a note window. FloatBoard can keep a small text-and-image working set above other windows. If you already have the note in another app, a window-pinning tool may be enough.

What should I try first?

Try Windows + V for reuse. If the real problem is losing sight of instructions, try FloatBoard with one labelled note and read the clipboard workspace guide. For code and screenshots, follow the separate UI debugging workflow.

title: How to Take Notes While Watching a Tutorial on One Screen
description: Use a timestamp, next-action note and screenshot to follow a software tutorial on one monitor. Compare split screen, PowerToys and floating notes.
alt: FloatBoard displaying image thumbnails next to a text panel containing an HTML reference snippet
caption: A FloatBoard text-and-image layout can hold references for a learning task. This existing product screenshot shows the interface, not a capture of the tutorial example below.
intro: When following a software tutorial on one screen, keep three things in your notes: the timestamp, the next action to try, and the result you expect. Pause to practise each step, then record what actually happened. A split-screen layout or a small floating note can keep those instructions visible beside your app without copying the entire lesson.

sections.title: Choose one result to reproduce
sections.html:
Before playing the tutorial, write down what you want to make: a responsive card, an image export or a spreadsheet formula. Record the tutorial URL and the software version used by the instructor if it is shown. Menu names and features can differ between versions.

For this example, suppose you are learning to build a card that changes from two columns to one on a narrow screen. You need the relevant breakpoint and layout rule, not a transcript of the whole video. Keep the completed exercise in your project folder.

sections.title: Split screen, PowerToys or FloatBoard?
sections.html:
Start with the layout that leaves your working app readable. The options below serve different needs; this is a FloatBoard product guide, not an independent comparative test.

Ways to keep tutorial instructions in sight
LayoutBest fitTrade-off
Side-by-side windowsWatching the instructor while practisingBoth apps need enough width to show their controls.
PowerToys Always On TopKeeping an existing note app visible on WindowsIt pins a window; your chosen app still handles the notes.
FloatBoardKeeping a short action note beside a screenshot or copied referenceA compact working set fits better than an entire lesson transcript.

With PowerToys installed and Always On Top enabled, select a note window and press Windows + Ctrl + T, the default shortcut, to toggle pinning. See Microsoft’s instructions, checked on 29 September 2026. If you changed the shortcut, use your configured combination.

sections.title: A tutorial note template you can copy
sections.html:
LESSON: [title + URL]
SOFTWARE: [app and version]
TIMESTAMP: [mm:ss]
GOAL: [one result]
NEXT ACTION: [one thing to try]
EXPECTED: [what should change]
ACTUAL: [what happened]
QUESTION: [what remains unclear]

For the responsive-card example, the next action could be: ‘Change the grid to one column below the chosen breakpoint.’ The expected result is: ‘Image appears above the text without horizontal scrolling.’ If it does not work, record the viewport width and the observed result before changing another rule.

The timestamp points back to the explanation. The actual-result line preserves your own observation. Keeping those separate helps you distinguish what the instructor said from what your project did.

sections.title: Follow a watch, pause, practise and check cycle
sections.html:
1. Watch one meaningful step. Stop when the instructor completes an action you can reproduce.
  2. Write the action in your own words. Copy a command only when exact spelling matters, and keep its source.
  3. Put the note in view. In FloatBoard, add your short text note, use the pin control and place the window beside your working area.
  4. Practise with the video paused. Return to your app and complete that single action.
  5. Compare the result. If a visual detail matters, keep one relevant screenshot alongside the note. Check small details in the original image.
  6. Record the outcome. Write what worked or the question to revisit, then advance to the next step.

Try this with one note and one image first. FloatBoard’s free plan has daily text and image limits, so use the board for the active step and your saved notes for the full lesson. The window does not need to contain every screenshot you take.

sections.title: What to do when the tutorial and your result differ
sections.html:
A menu item is missing: compare your software version with the lesson before trying unrelated commands. Note the version difference and consult that app’s documentation.

Your output looks different: compare at the same viewport size, zoom level or export setting. A screenshot without those conditions can lead you to fix the wrong thing.

The note covers a control: move or resize the note, or temporarily unpin it. If you constantly need to uncover the app, switch to side-by-side windows or pause the video more often.

You have too many unanswered questions: save them in the lesson document. Keep only the question blocking the current step in the floating note. For a reproducible interface problem, the code-and-screenshot debugging guide offers a more detailed evidence template.

sections.title: Turn the temporary note into a useful record
sections.html:
At the end of a lesson, save three things together: your exercise, the source URL with useful timestamps, and a short explanation of the step you can now perform. Move unresolved questions into that record before clearing the board.

Use screenshots you are allowed to retain and do not redistribute a paid course’s materials without permission. A screenshot can remind you where a control was, but your own explanation is what makes the note reusable when the interface changes.

sections.title: Questions about taking notes during tutorials
sections.html:
Should I write down everything the instructor says?

For a practical software task, begin with the action, expected result and question you need answered. Add background explanation when it changes how you perform the task. A full transcript can be useful for other purposes, but it is hard to use as a small on-screen checklist.

How can I take notes without a second monitor?

Pause the lesson while practising, use side-by-side windows when space allows, or keep a short note pinned above your app. Change the layout if it makes controls too small to use comfortably.

Does FloatBoard automatically transcribe or synchronize a video?

This workflow uses manually written notes, timestamps and selected image references. It does not depend on transcription, a video integration or automatic timestamp capture.

Can I use this for reading a written tutorial?

Yes. Replace the timestamp with the heading or section link. For longer reading and drafting, use the research notes workflow. To try the compact tutorial setup, download FloatBoard and start with a single next-action note.

caption: Four car-photo references in FloatBoard above the source page. The grid helps shortlist images while browsing; open the originals to judge detail or color.
intro: To compare photos side by side on Windows, start with Microsoft Photos’ multi-view if your pictures are already in one collection. Use Windows Snap for two full-size windows. If you are browsing several references while working in another app, keep a small image board visible and return to the originals for close inspection. This guide shows all three layouts and a four-photo comparison you can repeat.

sections.title: Decide what you are comparing before opening more photos
sections.html:
Choose one question: Which composition fits a project? Which lighting treatment should you study? Which of two exports preserves small details? The answer determines the layout. A grid of thumbnails can help you shortlist visual directions, but it is a poor place to judge sharpness, small text or exact colors.

For a fair comparison, choose images of a similar subject, angle and crop when possible. If the candidates have different framing or lighting, record that difference before treating it as a difference in the subject. Keep a link or filename for every original so you can inspect it again.

sections.title: Compare multiple local photos in Microsoft Photos
sections.html:
1. Open the current Microsoft Photos app and navigate to the folder containing your candidates.
  2. Open one photo, then use the filmstrip to select the other photos you want to view in multi-view.
  3. Compare the same feature in each image, such as a crop, reflection or edge detail. Return to a larger view before making a decision about fine quality.

Microsoft documents multi-view in the new Photos app as a way to compare photos and videos side by side by selecting items in the filmstrip. Its interface may differ if you have Photos Legacy or an older app version. This built-in option is a good starting point when the originals are local and you do not need them above a separate working app. Documentation checked on 1 October 2026.

sections.title: Use Windows Snap for two large images or browser pages
sections.html:
When you need to read details at a larger size, open the two originals in separate windows. These could be two browser windows showing source pages or an image viewer beside the app where you work. Select the first window and press Windows + Left Arrow; select the second and press Windows + Right Arrow. Resize the divider or use the available Snap layout to leave enough room for both images.

Microsoft’s Snap guide also describes dragging windows to screen edges or corners and filling the remaining space with Snap Assist. This layout is useful for checking two full-size views. If you keep switching among four candidates, narrow the set to two finalists before examining small details.

sections.title: Keep a short image shortlist visible while you browse
sections.html:
The screenshot above shows a real FloatBoard layout: four car images in a two-by-two grid, with larger source photos visible in the browser behind it. Use this kind of board when your task is to keep a few references in sight while you browse, draw or write—not to replace the original files or pages.

  1. Save each source URL or original filename in your project notes. Use images you are allowed to keep and share.
  2. Add two to four candidate images to FloatBoard using the image workflow in your installed version. The free plan currently allows five images per day and one window.
  3. Position the board where it does not cover the feature you are comparing, then use its pin control and return to your browser or work app.
  4. Give the candidates simple names in your project note—A, B, C and D—and write one useful observation for each. The labels belong in your note; this screenshot does not show labels on the image tiles.
  5. Open a source image at full size whenever a thumbnail leaves a question unresolved. Keep the final choice and its source in your project folder.

FloatBoard can also show text notes, so a short decision checklist can sit with the images. For a larger searchable collection of references, use a dedicated asset library and bring only the current shortlist to the floating board. The reference-image organization guide explains that longer-term setup.

sections.title: Example: shortlist four car-photo references without confusing lighting with design
sections.html:
Suppose you are choosing a visual reference for an illustration of a car. In the screenshot, one image is an outdoor silver-car shot, another shows a blue car in a warm courtyard, a third has a dark convertible against a neutral background, and a fourth shows a bright yellow car in a courtyard. They are different scenes and viewpoints, so this is a shortlist for art direction, not a controlled test of vehicle shape or paint color.

What the four-image grid can help you decide
QuestionCompare in the gridVerify in the original
CompositionHow much space surrounds the car and where the visual weight falls.Whether the crop hides a part needed for your drawing.
LightingDaylight, warm courtyard light or a more neutral backdrop.Highlight edges and shadow detail at a larger size.
Color directionWhich broad palette supports the mood you want.Original file, exposure and color settings before choosing exact values.

If your question is about wheel shape, compare photos taken from a similar angle. If it is about color, do not assume the blue and yellow courtyard shots have matching light. The useful result of a first pass is a smaller set of candidates and a clearer next question, not a verdict from four tiny tiles.

sections.title: Photos, Snap, a pinned viewer or FloatBoard: which fits the task?
sections.html:
These are different ways to arrange what you see, not a speed benchmark. The Windows and PowerToys descriptions are based on Microsoft documentation checked on 1 October 2026; FloatBoard publishes this guide.

Choose a comparison layout
SetupUse it whenLimit to remember
Microsoft Photos multi-viewYour originals are local and you want several images in one viewer.The interface depends on which Photos version is installed.
Windows SnapYou need two larger windows or two source pages side by side.Each window gets less screen width, especially on a small display.
PowerToys Always On TopYou already have a suitable image viewer and want to pin its window above another app.It pins the viewer; it does not create an image library or comparison grid.
FloatBoardYou want a compact shortlist of images, with optional text notes, visible while you use another app.Use the originals for zoomed detail and check the free-plan limits.

If you need aligned zoom, an overlay or pixel differences between nearly identical exports, use a tool built for precise image comparison. FloatBoard’s grid is for visible references; it does not calculate differences, rank images or verify that two files are duplicates.

sections.title: Avoid four common mistakes when comparing image references
sections.html:
• Comparing unlike crops: match the subject and framing before drawing conclusions about proportions. A low camera angle can make a shape look different.
  • Judging exact color from a thumbnail: browser scaling, display settings and the source image can all affect what you see. Open the original in an appropriate editor when color accuracy matters.
  • Losing the source: write down the file path or page URL before closing the browser. A temporary board is not a project archive.
  • Reusing an image without permission: collecting a visual reference does not grant publication rights. Check the source and license before you put a photo in a public deliverable.

When a decision matters, record why you chose the finalist. For example: ‘Use the neutral-background image to study silhouette; keep the courtyard image only for warm lighting.’ That is more useful than a folder of unnamed thumbnails.

sections.title: Questions about comparing photos side by side
sections.html:
How do I compare two photos side by side in Windows 11?

Use Microsoft Photos multi-view for pictures in its filmstrip, or put two image windows side by side with Windows Snap. Choose Photos when you want a single viewer and Snap when you need separate windows or source pages.

Can I compare images from a website without making a collage?

Yes. Open the source pages in separate browser windows and use Snap, or keep a few allowed reference images in a small floating board while the browser stays open. You do not need to export a combined image just to make a decision.

Can I keep reference photos on top of another app?

On Windows, PowerToys Always On Top can pin an existing viewer. FloatBoard has its own pin control and can keep a small image grid beside optional notes. Move the pinned window if it blocks your work.

Does FloatBoard detect differences between two images?

No. This workflow uses human visual comparison of a small reference set. For pixel-level differences, synchronized zoom or duplicate detection, use a dedicated image-comparison tool and inspect the original files.

What if I need to organize hundreds of photos?

Keep those files in a searchable photo library or project folder. Use FloatBoard only for the few candidates you are actively considering, then save the final decision and source back in the project record. See the guide to organizing reference images for that distinction.

sections.title: Try the two-minute comparison
sections.html:
Pick one real question and two candidate images. Try Microsoft Photos or Snap first. If you need the candidates to remain visible while editing or browsing, try FloatBoard with a small pinned set and one note about the decision. Open the originals before you commit to the choice, then clear the temporary board when the task is done.

If your main problem is keeping instructions visible rather than comparing images, the floating-notes guide covers that workflow.

title: How to Copy Text from a Screenshot on Windows and Check It Against the Original
description: Extract text from a Windows screenshot with Snipping Tool or PowerToys, then compare the result with the image before using it in a form, note or report.
alt: FloatBoard displaying four image thumbnails beside a text card containing HTML reference text
caption: This FloatBoard screenshot shows a mixed image-and-text layout. It does not show OCR or the Windows text-extraction tools.
intro: A screenshot looks like text, but its letters are pixels. On Windows, Snipping Tool or PowerToys can turn those pixels into copyable text. The extra step that matters is checking the result against the image before it reaches a form, document or message. This guide walks through both extraction options and a small comparison workflow that keeps the source in view.

sections.title: Keep the screenshot as the source of truth
sections.html:
Before extracting anything, save or locate the original screenshot. Give it a useful name, such as shipping-error-2026-10-02.png, and keep it in the project folder. The copied words are a draft transcription; the image is the evidence of what appeared on screen.

If the screenshot contains names, addresses, account numbers or other private information, crop to the smallest relevant area before sharing it. For this guide, imagine a harmless sample image of a shipping form with the message “Pickup is unavailable for this address.” The example contains no real customer data. If the message exists as selectable text in the app, copy that text directly instead of running OCR on its screenshot.

Decide which part you need: the whole message, one field label or a reference number. A tight selection makes the later comparison easier. Keep punctuation and capitalization when exact wording matters, especially for error reports and instructions.

sections.title: Copy words from a screenshot with Snipping Tool
sections.html:
1. Display the screenshot at a readable size, or leave the original content visible on screen. Press Windows + Shift + S and select the relevant area.
  2. Open the new capture in Snipping Tool.
  3. Select Text actions. Select the exact words you need, or choose Copy all text for the whole snip.
  4. Paste into a plain note or draft field. Read the pasted result beside the screenshot before using it elsewhere.

Microsoft’s Snipping Tool instructions document the screenshot shortcut and Text actions, including selection and Copy all text. They describe this as optical character recognition (OCR) and say text recognition happens locally on the device. Interface labels can vary with the installed version, so update Snipping Tool if the option is missing and check Microsoft’s current instructions.

Copy all text is convenient for a single block. For a crowded dialog, select only the sentence you need; copying every label, button and footer can produce a confusing draft.

sections.title: Extract text already visible on screen with PowerToys
sections.html:
If you have Microsoft PowerToys installed and Text Extractor enabled, leave the screenshot visible and press Windows + Shift + T, its default shortcut. Drag a rectangle around the words. PowerToys copies the recognized text to the clipboard; paste it into a note, then compare it with the image. Press Esc to leave capture mode without selecting anything.

The PowerToys Text Extractor documentation covers the shortcut, selection and clipboard behavior. It warns that recognized text may be imperfect and needs proofreading. The default OCR language follows Windows language settings; the page also explains language packs if recognition fails for a language you need.

PowerToys is useful when the text sits inside an image, video frame or another visible app and you want a quick rectangular capture. Snipping Tool is the more direct choice when you also need to save a screenshot. Microsoft specifically recommends Snipping Tool for screenshot capture. Neither tool makes the OCR result an authoritative copy of the original.

sections.title: Compare the OCR result with the original, character by character
sections.html:
Put the screenshot and pasted text next to each other. Read the image first, then the extracted text. Start with the characters most likely to change the meaning: numbers, negative words, dates, punctuation, capitalization and lookalike letters such as O and 0. For multi-line text, confirm that OCR kept the lines in the right order. Do not silently “fix” a phrase from memory when the image is unclear; zoom in or return to the app that produced it.

Here is a fictional example of the shipping-form message. It illustrates a possible OCR mistake, not an observed result from either Microsoft tool.

Check each copied fragment against the screenshot
In the sample screenshotIllustrative OCR draftAction
Pickup is unavailablePickup is availableRestore “unavailable”; the missing prefix reverses the meaning.
for this address.for this addressRestore the final period if recording the exact message.
Try another delivery option.Try another delivery option.Keep this line; it matches.

Once corrected, label the note Verified against screenshot and keep the original filename or path with it. For a bug report, quote the corrected message and attach the screenshot as evidence. For a customer-facing response or an official record, verify the wording in the source system as well: a screenshot may be cropped, outdated or missing context.

sections.title: Keep the image and corrected text visible while you work
sections.html:
For a short task, two ordinary windows side by side may be enough: screenshot on one side, destination document on the other. If you repeatedly switch to another app, a small floating reference can keep the comparison nearby. FloatBoard lets you place an image and a text note in one visible working board, as the product image above illustrates. Add the screenshot as the image reference, then add a labelled text note with the checked wording and the source filename.

FloatBoard does not perform OCR in this workflow. Extract the text in Snipping Tool or PowerToys first, then paste the verified result into a FloatBoard text note if keeping it visible helps. Its clipboard history can help with recent copies, while the visible board keeps the image and checked note together. Save the authoritative screenshot and final text in your project files; a temporary board should not be the only copy.

If you mainly need to retrieve a recent copy, the Windows clipboard history guide covers that workflow. For a reference that must remain in view, see the floating notes guide. Use only material you are comfortable showing if you share your screen.

sections.title: Recognize the limits before relying on copied text
sections.html:
OCR can stumble on small type, low contrast, motion blur, unusual fonts, rotated text and overlapping interface elements. It may insert a line break in the middle of a sentence, join separate columns or omit a short word. The PowerToys documentation explicitly calls for proofreading; apply that habit whichever extractor you use.

A cropped screenshot can hide the preceding instruction or the label that gives a number its meaning. Keep enough context to verify what the text refers to, while avoiding unnecessary personal data. If a critical character remains unreadable, return to the source app, enlarge the image or request a clearer source. Do not guess at amounts, dates, codes or addresses.

Remember that copying OCR text changes its form, not its trustworthiness. Treat it as a transcription you have checked for your stated purpose. If an app supplies accessible, selectable text, use that source when possible.

sections.title: Questions about copying text from screenshots
sections.html:
Can I copy text from a screenshot without installing PowerToys?

Yes. Snipping Tool’s Text actions can extract text from a snip. Follow Microsoft’s current Snipping Tool instructions and check that your installed version offers the control.

Why did PowerToys copy the wrong words?

Try a tighter capture around the relevant line and enlarge the screenshot before extracting. Check the configured OCR language if the text uses another language. Proofread the result against the image; a second pass does not guarantee accuracy.

Is a screenshot or the extracted text better for an error report?

Keep both. The screenshot shows visual context; verified, selectable text makes the exact message easier to quote and search. Add the action that triggered the error, but exclude private fields. For a code and screenshot debugging example, see the UI bug guide.

Does FloatBoard recognize text inside an image?

No OCR feature is claimed here. Use a Windows text-extraction tool for recognition. FloatBoard can keep the screenshot and your verified text note visible together while you complete the task. Try FloatBoard if that visible reference would help.

title: How to Keep Meeting Notes Visible During a Video Call
description: Keep an agenda and action list in sight during a Teams video call. Set up a personal note, use collaborative meeting notes for the shared record, and share your screen safely.
alt: FloatBoard window with text cards on the left and image thumbnails on the right
caption: This FloatBoard screenshot shows a mixed text-and-image layout. It is not a capture of a video call or the meeting-note example below.
intro: To keep meeting notes visible during a video call, prepare a short personal checklist before the call, place it beside the meeting window, and record decisions and actions in the team's shared notes. If you use Microsoft Teams, its collaborative Notes can hold the agenda and official follow-up tasks; a small pinned FloatBoard window can hold your own prompts while you speak.

sections.title: Decide what belongs in the shared record
sections.html:
Before arranging windows, decide which notes need to be visible to the whole meeting. A shared agenda, agreed decision, task owner and due date should live in the meeting record. Your private prompts might be a question you must ask, a figure to verify or the order in which you want to present. Do not leave the only copy of an action in a personal scratchpad.

Microsoft's Teams meeting notes guide says attendees can add an agenda, notes and tasks that others can see and edit. Changes appear live, and notes remain available after the meeting. In Teams, open Notes from the meeting controls. You can prepare an agenda from the calendar before the meeting too. Access can vary: Microsoft says external attendees cannot access or edit meeting notes. If your call includes guests, agree on a record they can actually receive.

Use a personal visible note for your own attention, not as a substitute for that shared record. This is a manual workflow published by FloatBoard.

sections.title: Arrange the call, shared notes and your prompt card
sections.html:
1. Open the shared agenda first. In Teams, select Notes and check that the agenda is the one for this meeting. Microsoft also documents an Open in new window option for meeting Notes, Chat and Copilot, so you can move or resize meeting content while the call continues.
  2. Make room for the conversation. Keep the speaker or shared presentation large enough to follow. Teams can reduce the meeting to a smaller window when you switch to another app; its controls remain available there. On one screen, avoid stacking so many panels that neither the speaker nor the task list is readable.
  3. Place your personal note. Add a short agenda or question list to FloatBoard, enable its pin control and put it beside the call. The floating-notes guide explains the text-and-image board. A single text card is enough for most meetings; an image is useful only if you genuinely need a visual reference.
  4. Rehearse a window switch. Click the call, shared notes and the document you may present. Confirm that your note stays readable without covering mute, leave or share controls. If it blocks the meeting, shrink it or use a side-by-side layout.

sections.title: Copy a compact agenda and action template
sections.html:
Start with a note you can scan while somebody else is talking. The example below is fictitious. Replace every bracketed field before the call; leave the decision and action lines blank until the group confirms them.

MEETING: [topic] — [date]
OUTCOME NEEDED: [one decision or result]
AGENDA: 1. [question]  2. [choice]  3. [next step]
ASK: [one question I must not forget]
DECISION: [what the group agreed, or pending]
ACTION: [verb + deliverable]
OWNER: [one named person]
DUE: [date and time zone, or agreed milestone]
OPEN: [unresolved question + who will answer]

For example, a release-planning call might end with: Decision: move the checklist review to Friday; Action: send the revised checklist; Owner: Maya; Due: 9 October, 15:00 Casablanca time. That is a sample format, not a report of a real meeting. Use an explicit date when possible; “next week” becomes unclear after the call. If the group cannot choose an owner or due date, mark it pending and ask before ending the meeting.

Keep the personal card to one small working set. Put detailed background and final outcomes in Teams Notes or the team's approved project document. If you need to keep a source beside a draft after the call, the research-notes workflow covers that separate task.

sections.title: Capture the decision without trying to transcribe everything
sections.html:
During discussion, write keywords that help you ask the next question. When a decision sounds settled, read it back: “We are choosing option B for Friday's review. Is that right?” Record the confirmed wording in the shared notes. If someone volunteers to act, ask for the deliverable and date as well as their name. “Maya will send the revised checklist by 9 October” is usable; “Maya to follow up” is not.

Separate a proposal from an agreement. A useful shorthand is Proposed, Decided and Open. A proposal can remain on your personal card until the group resolves it; agreed work belongs in the meeting record. If the conversation moves quickly, write a short placeholder and return to it before the call ends. Avoid guessing what a quiet participant accepted.

Teams meeting notes let participants tag people in agenda and task items, according to Microsoft's instructions. If your organization uses that workflow, add the agreed owner there. A name on a private floating note does not assign a task in Teams.

sections.title: Check what people will see before you share
sections.html:
A visible personal board can also be visible to other people if you share the whole display. Before selecting Share, remove sensitive prompts, customer details and private links from the screen. Microsoft says Teams can present either an entire screen or a chosen window. Choose the window containing the material you intend to show when that fits the presentation, and inspect the preview or ask a trusted colleague what is visible. Do not assume that a pinned note is private merely because it sits outside your slide or browser content.

Pause before changing what you share. If you need to switch documents, stop sharing, arrange the new window and start again with the intended selection. This is a practical privacy precaution, not a guarantee that a particular operating system or calling app will always isolate every overlay. If an image on your board includes confidential information, remove or redact it before the call.

sections.title: Choose the simplest visible-note setup for your call
sections.html:
The options answer different needs. This is a FloatBoard product guide, not an independent performance test. The Teams and PowerToys descriptions are based on linked Microsoft documentation checked on 2 October 2026.

Where each meeting note belongs
SetupBest useLimit to remember
Teams collaborative NotesShared agenda, live decisions and assigned follow-up tasks.It is visible to eligible meeting participants; Microsoft says external attendees cannot access or edit these notes.
PowerToys Always On TopOn Windows, pin the notes app you already use. The default shortcut is Windows + Ctrl + T.It pins a window; that notes app still stores and organizes its content.
FloatBoardKeep a small personal text checklist and optional image reference above other apps while you follow the call.It is a personal working board, with no automatic transcription or Teams synchronization. See the current plan limits.

On a crowded display, Teams Notes in its own window may be enough. If you already have a suitable note app on Windows, PowerToys can pin it. Choose FloatBoard when you want a compact text-and-image prompt card that remains in sight as you move between the call and other work.

sections.title: Finish with an agreed record and clear your prompt card
sections.html:
Reserve the last minute to read out the decisions and action list. Confirm each deliverable, owner and due date, including a time zone where it matters. Record any unresolved point as an open question with the person who will answer it. Then check that the shared notes show the agreed version, rather than only your shorthand.

After the call, return to the saved meeting record or your team's project system to correct obvious gaps. Keep relevant links there. Remove obsolete or sensitive text from the personal board before your next screen share. FloatBoard's role was to keep the next prompt visible during the conversation; the persistent record belongs where your team expects to find it.

If this arrangement helps, download FloatBoard and try it with one short meeting card. For notes you copied earlier and need to retrieve, see the separate clipboard-history comparison.

sections.title: Frequently asked questions about visible meeting notes
sections.html:
Can I keep my notes visible without a second monitor?

Yes. Reduce the call to a smaller view where your meeting app supports it, pop out its notes, or put a compact note beside the call. Keep faces, shared content and controls readable; if an overlay hides them, switch to side-by-side windows or a paper checklist.

Are FloatBoard notes the same as Teams meeting notes?

No. Teams Notes are collaborative meeting content for eligible participants. FloatBoard holds a personal working set of text and images on your desktop. Copy confirmed decisions into the shared record yourself; there is no automatic sync or transcription in this workflow.

Will a pinned note appear when I share my screen?

It may appear if you share your whole display. If you share a specific window, check the preview and the actual participant view before relying on that selection for privacy. Clear sensitive material before presenting.

What should an action item include?

Write a concrete deliverable, one owner and an agreed due date. Add an open question when a decision is pending. Confirm the wording aloud and place the final item in the team's shared notes or task system.

title: How to Keep a Web Image Reference Visible While You Browse
description: Keep one useful web image in sight while researching without losing its source. A practical workflow for designers using a floating image reference.
alt: Recorded FloatBoard demo beside a browser search for landscape photography, with a selected reference image shown in a larger view
caption: Recorded Linux demo from July 2026: one landscape reference stays beside the browser as the search continues. The current interface may differ; this recording later contains more images than the free plan permits per day.
demo_alt: Recorded FloatBoard demo showing a landscape web image opened as a working reference while browsing continues
intro: When you are looking through web images for a design, the useful picture often disappears as soon as you open another result. The simple fix is to separate the page you are researching from the one image you are studying. Keep a record of the original page, show a working copy beside your browser, and ask one concrete question of it. This guide explains that one-image workflow, when a floating board helps, and when to return to the original file instead.

sections.title: Give the reference one specific job
sections.html:
Start with a decision, not an instruction to collect everything attractive on the page. Imagine that you are designing a landing page with a broad landscape photograph behind a short headline. Your question might be: Does this image leave enough calm space for the text? A single candidate can answer that question. You do not yet need a gallery, a mood board or a permanent image library.

Look at the photograph in its source context first. Note the subject, horizon and area where text could sit. If the image seems relevant, keep it visible while you examine other candidates. You can then judge whether a new result solves the same problem better instead of trusting a vague memory of the first. This is a small working comparison across time, even though only one image is on your board at once.

sections.title: Record the source before leaving the page
sections.html:
Before opening another result, put two things in a scratch note: a link to the page and a short visual label. For example, “A — low ridge with empty sky; possible headline area.” When a page contains a gallery, note which image you mean. A link to a page with thirty thumbnails is much less useful if you cannot identify the candidate later.

Keep this note next to your design question. As you browse, compare each new result against A on that question alone: does it offer more uninterrupted sky, a cleaner horizon or a better subject position? If yes, replace the working reference and relabel the note. If no, move on. The link is a way back to the source, and you should still check the source's usage terms before putting any image in published work. For now, it mainly prevents your search from turning into an anonymous sequence of pictures.

sections.title: Put a working copy beside your browser
sections.html:
With the source recorded, add the image to FloatBoard using the image workflow supported by your installed version. Place its window at the side of the browser and enable always-on-top if you want the picture to remain in view when another browser tab receives focus. The recorded demo above shows the broad idea on Linux: a web landscape is visible in the app while the browser continues through more results. The app's controls can change between versions, so use the controls in your current build rather than copying a video gesture exactly.

Keep the reference small enough that the search results remain usable. If the window covers the next candidate, move or resize it. On a narrow screen, alternate between the source page and your reference instead of squeezing both until neither is readable. FloatBoard is a working surface for a few live references, not the only place to store project assets.

sections.title: Write down what the image actually contributes
sections.html:
Add one short note in your project document: source, useful detail, design implication. For the landscape example: “Source page X; open sky above the ridge; headline could sit in the sky if contrast holds at the target crop.” This records an observation rather than a promise that the image will work. It also helps you discard an image later without losing the reason you selected it.

Distinguish the photographer's caption from your own description. When you copy text from a source page, mark it as a quotation and keep the link beside it. If you cannot state what the picture helps you decide, it may be pleasant browsing rather than a useful reference. Return to the design question and either replace the image or stop collecting for a moment to make a draft.

sections.title: Check the original at the size that matters
sections.html:
When one image seems promising, pause browsing and put it in the layout you are actually designing. A photograph with a generous sky in the browser can lose that space when a wide hero is cropped into a phone-sized panel. Try the real headline and button over the image; check whether they cover the subject or become hard to read. Make one note about the result, such as “desktop works, mobile crop loses the ridge.”

If the concern is fine detail, open the source at an appropriate size instead of zooming a tiny board preview. If the concern is composition, draw a rough crop boundary or test the layout directly. These are different checks. Do not reject a useful composition solely because the floating window is small, and do not approve a final crop solely because its thumbnail looks calm. The working reference keeps your thought in sight; the design canvas settles the decision.

sections.title: Know when one reference should become a shortlist
sections.html:
One visible reference works while you search for a better answer to one question. It stops working when the task changes to comparing multiple dimensions simultaneously. If you need to decide among a few different visual directions, build a deliberate shortlist and name each candidate's role. The landscape hero-image shortlist explains how to move from browsing to a decision. For a broader design research library, see the reference image organizer guide.

Do not let the demo's later multi-image view define the free plan. The recorded session includes more images than the current free plan's five images per day. Check the current limits before starting a larger session, and keep originals in a separate folder regardless of the plan you use.

sections.title: Finish the session with a decision and a retrievable file
sections.html:
End the search with a one-line decision rather than a board full of unexplained candidates. Write “keep A for desktop draft,” “replace A with B because the mobile crop is cleaner,” or “no candidate answers the brief; search for a lower horizon.” If A moves forward, place its page link beside that decision so you can retrieve the exact image. If it fails, record the failed criterion; that becomes the next search query.

Do a five-minute layout test before starting another round of browsing. Seeing the candidate behind real content often reveals that the problem is the headline placement, not the photograph. In that case, adjusting the layout may be more productive than collecting more pictures. If you do need several distinct candidates at once, switch to the hero-image shortlist workflow and give each a clear role. A one-image pin is best while you are testing one hypothesis.

sections.title: Frequently asked questions
sections.html:
How can I keep a picture visible when I change browser tabs?

Use a small always-on-top image window next to the browser, or arrange two windows on the desktop. Leave enough room to inspect new results; the reference should support browsing, not cover it.

What if the floating window blocks the next result?

Move or resize it, or briefly hide it during a closer look. Returning to the same reference is more useful than keeping it permanently in the way.

When should one reference become a shortlist?

When you need to compare different solutions at the same time. Choose a few candidates with distinct roles rather than accumulating similar images as you scroll.

title: How to Shortlist Landscape Photos for a Website Hero Image
description: Choose landscape hero-image candidates by crop, text space, visual direction and rights. Build a small photo shortlist instead of collecting endlessly.
alt: Recorded FloatBoard demo showing a small grid of landscape candidate images while browsing a photography website
caption: Recorded Linux demo from July 2026: landscape candidates appear in a compact FloatBoard grid beside web results. The current interface may differ, and this recording later shows more images than the free plan permits per day.
demo_alt: Recorded demo of building a small landscape-photo working grid next to browser results
intro: A website hero image has a harder job than simply looking good. It must support the message, survive desktop and mobile crops, leave space for readable text and be usable under the source license. This guide is for a designer choosing a landscape photograph for one hero section. It uses a small visible shortlist to make the choice explicit, then checks the finalists in the actual layout. It is deliberately narrower than building a general inspiration board.

sections.title: Write the hero-image brief before opening a photo site
sections.html:
Describe the page in one sentence: what does the visitor need to understand, and what action should follow? Then list the image constraints. For a travel landing page, you might need an open horizon, a calm right side for a headline, a subject that remains recognizable on a phone, and a tone that fits the brand. These constraints are more useful than “find something beautiful.”

Decide whether the image must show a real place, a mood or a product context. A scenic photograph that implies the wrong destination can mislead. If the hero contains text, identify its likely position before you browse. If the page will be localized into longer languages, allow more room than the English mockup appears to need. Write these facts in a project note so each candidate faces the same test.

sections.title: Choose candidates with different reasons to win
sections.html:
Shortlist three or four images that test different approaches, rather than four nearly identical mountain photos. One might offer open sky for text, another a strong foreground that communicates place, and a third a softer palette that supports navigation. Give each a one-line role. The goal is to learn which visual direction works, not to fill every empty slot on the board.

Keep a link to each source page and, where available, the creator and license details. Before bringing an image into a review board, check that you can identify its origin. A search page is a discovery tool; it is not the source record. If the only copy you can find is a repost or tiny preview, set it aside until the original is located. Otherwise you risk making a layout around an asset you cannot responsibly use.

sections.title: Use a compact grid to compare overall direction
sections.html:
A small grid helps you scan composition and contrast quickly. Add your selected working copies to FloatBoard using your installed version's image controls, then keep the window beside the browser or design app. The recorded demo above shows landscapes collected into a compact grid during a web search. Use the current app interface as it exists today; the recording is from July 2026 on Linux and should not be treated as a feature walkthrough for every platform.

Label candidates in your own project note by source and role: A: open sky, B: human scale, C: dark foreground. Avoid calling an image “best” before testing the crop. If the working grid becomes too small to judge even composition, remove weaker candidates. The current free plan is limited to five images per day; the later recorded board contains more than that, so plan your shortlist against the current plan details.

sections.title: Test every finalist in the real hero crop
sections.html:
Move from the board into the page layout for the actual decision. Put each candidate behind the real headline, button and navigation. Check a wide desktop viewport and a narrow phone viewport. A dramatic mountain peak can disappear at mobile width; a person can fall beneath a button; a dark region that helped white text on desktop can shift out of frame on mobile. Record the failure or success for each crop, not just a gut feeling about the original.

Do not use the board thumbnail as a color or sharpness test. Open the original asset at adequate resolution for that review. Check that the supplied file can support the intended size without obvious softness, and look for compression artifacts around high-contrast edges. Keep a neutral backup plan, such as a solid-color hero, if no photograph survives the functional checks. The design needs clarity more than it needs a scenic image.

sections.title: Judge text readability without hiding the image
sections.html:
Test the actual words, not placeholder text. The longest likely headline and the button label expose collisions that a two-word mockup hides. Check light and dark areas behind each line at both viewport sizes. You may need a gradient overlay, a text panel or a different photo. The overlay should support legibility without making the image muddy or concealing the subject that justified choosing it.

Ask a colleague who has not seen the shortlist to read the page for its message first, then describe what the image contributes. If they focus only on the photograph, it may be overpowering the content. If they cannot read the heading immediately, the crop or treatment is not ready. This simple review is more useful than a debate over which picture has the most impressive subject.

sections.title: Confirm that the finalist can actually be published
sections.html:
Before the team approves a hero, revisit the source page for the chosen file. Read the site's current license and any additional restrictions attached to the image. Note the creator, source URL, permission terms and download date. If the use involves recognizable people, logos or sensitive property, check whether further permissions are needed for your particular commercial context. A visible “download” button is not a blanket clearance for every use.

Save the original file and the source record together. Do not flatten the project into a screenshot from a browser; it can lose resolution and provenance. If a finalist fails the rights check, choose a licensed alternative from the shortlist or return to search. It is cheaper to make that change before the design is approved than after artwork and copy are built around the image.

sections.title: Choose one winner and record why
sections.html:
Use a brief decision table in your project document: candidate, hero message fit, desktop crop, mobile crop, text space, asset and rights status. Mark each item with a short observation, not a pseudo-precise score. For example: “A: strong open sky, but subject disappears on phone”; “B: subject holds on both, needs a light text panel.” This exposes the tradeoff instead of letting the most recent image win by accident.

When one candidate wins, move it into the actual design and retain the source record. Archive the other links in your project notes if they might help a later page, but clear the temporary board.
